title: Development server and proxy route registry
description: The enumerated declaration `scripts/template/proxy-contract.ts` validates. A development proxy can be structurally perfect and silently nonfunctional: a string-shorthand target never forwards a WebSocket upgrade, a route that rewrites its path cannot forward one either, and a server bound to the container's loopback is unreachable through the one published port. So the surface is declared here — the server, the preview server, the HMR policy, the host allowlist, the route table and its upstreams — and reconciled against the tree and against the worktree runtime contract. `mode` is the load-bearing field: `skeleton` asserts, positively, that no Vite configuration and no proxy surface exists anywhere in the tracked tree; `active` asserts the declared config file exists and runs every rule over it.

mode.description: The declared tree state. It is compared with the derived state before any other rule runs, and a disagreement in either direction is the first error.

configPath.description: The one Vite configuration file this registry governs. In `active` mode it must exist, be an ordinary in-tree file with exactly one hard link, and canonicalize inside the repository — a guard that reads a symlink or a hardlinked twin validates a file it does not own.

runtime.description: The runtime the development server runs under. It is declared rather than inferred because a WebSocket proxy's correctness depends on it: a forwarder built on `node:http` compatibility can fire its upgrade event and then never flush a byte back to the real client, which presents as a hang and not as an error. A runtime whose upgrade forwarding is unproven, declared beside a route that forwards WebSockets, is a refusal that a reasoned waiver may lift.

wsRuntimeWaiver.description: The reasoned waiver that lifts the runtime refusal, or null. A waiver keeps the finding a decision rather than an obstacle: the guard prints the reason it was given, so the next reader inherits the argument instead of rediscovering the defect.

publishedContainerPort.description: The single container port that crosses the host boundary. Declared here and reconciled with `scripts/worktree/contract.toml` when that file exists, because a gated guard must not hard-depend on a file another capability owns.

friendlyDomainPattern.description: The friendly host pattern the worktree runtime publishes alongside the direct origin. Both origins are browser-visible at once, which is why a pinned HMR client port is a refusal rather than a convenience.

server.description: The development server, or null in skeleton mode.

preview.description: The preview server, or null in skeleton mode. Its route table must match the development server's exactly: a route present in one and absent from the other is a surface that works in development and disappears in preview.

routes.description: The one route table both servers declare. It is shared rather than duplicated so that alignment is a property of the declaration rather than a rule somebody has to remember.

upstreams.description: Every loopback port a route may target. A route whose target port is not declared here is a route to a service nothing in this project owns.

path.description: The path prefix this route matches, always absolute.

target.description: An absolute loopback origin. A target that names a public host is an unintended external call, and one bound to 0.0.0.0 is not an address a client connects to.

ws.description: Whether this route forwards the WebSocket upgrade. Declared explicitly on every route and never defaulted, because the defect this registry exists to catch is invisible: a route that answers HTTP correctly and drops every upgrade.

changeOrigin.description: Declared explicitly rather than defaulted. A route that never states whether it rewrites the Host header has not decided.

secure.description: Declared explicitly rather than defaulted. Disabling certificate verification against an https target is a refusal.

rewrite.description: The path rewrite, or null. A rewrite beside a forwarded upgrade is structurally valid and nonfunctional: path rewriting and WebSocket upgrade forwarding do not compose.

host.description: The bind address. A server bound to the container's loopback is unreachable through a published port, so this is `true` or the wide bind — and the pairing of a wide bind with a strict host allowlist is the whole safety argument.

strictPort.description: Pinned true. Without it the server silently takes the next free port and the container publish maps to nothing, which is why a stale listener can pass a health gate against the wrong server.

allowedHosts.description: The host allowlist. It is a Cross-Site WebSocket Hijacking defense and not a convenience: a WebSocket handshake is not subject to CORS, so a cross-site page can open an authenticated socket unless the server checks the host itself.

hmr.description: The HMR override, or null. Null is the correct value in this runtime and the inverse of the advice everybody gives: two origins are browser-visible at once, a pinned client port is a single number, and it can match at most one of them while silently breaking the other. A non-null override carries the reason it was needed.

origin.description: The asset origin override, or null. It carries the same defect a pinned HMR client port does, one layer over: a single absolute origin written into generated asset URLs is wrong for whichever of the two published origins it is not.

frontedBy.description: The declared service that binds the published container port in front of this server, or null when the server binds it itself. Exactly one process binds that port, and a service named here must exist in the worktree runtime contract's service list.
